                COMPLAINT REQUESTING FAST-TRACK PROCESSING

       During Winter Storm Fern in late January to early February 2026, PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. (“PJM” or “Respondent”), in the name of reliability, undertook massive advance scheduling

of gas-fired generating units.1 The public record and documents available to Complainant

Monongahela Power Company (“Mon Power” or “Complainant”) demonstrate that Mon Power,

and ultimately its retail customers in West Virginia, suffered substantial harm—approximately

$145 million—due to an extreme divergence between (a) the Locational Marginal Prices (“LMPs”)

at the nodes where Mon Power sells power from its coal-fired generating units, and (b) the LMP

at the node where Mon Power buys power to serve its retail customer load. Unlike typical

reliability-driven uplift costs that are allocated across all of PJM based upon load-ratio share, this




1

Market reliability scheduling and commitment practices, including pre-scheduling, advance
scheduling, advance commitments, and any related operator-initiated or out-of-market
commitments, instructions, uplift treatment, or settlement consequences associated with resources
scheduled or committed before or outside the ordinary Day-Ahead Market clearing process, even
if such resource unit participated in and cleared in the Day-Ahead Market or Real-Time Market.
 $145 million will, absent the Commission’s intervention, be left for ordinary West Virginia citizens

to bear at a time when electricity affordability is already a serious problem.

        A full picture of PJM’s actions and whether they violated PJM’s tariff is not possible

without discovery of PJM’s unit-level, offer, commitment, uplift, congestion, settlement, and

market-simulation data. But the public record already gives rise to a substantial concern that

warrants further investigation, and Mon Power therefore requests that the Commission set this

Complaint for hearing to assess whether PJM’s advance-scheduling and commitment practices,

Day-Ahead Market treatment, uplift payments, congestion impacts, and settlement treatment

during Winter Storm Fern violated or misapplied the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and

Operating Agreement by exceeding and/or misusing PJM’s limited advance-scheduling and

commitment authority, producing unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential

outcomes, and/or outcomes that are inconsistent with cost-causation principles.

        Pursuant to Federal Power Act (“FPA”) sections 206, 306, and 3092 and Rule 206 of the

Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Commission,3 Mon Power hereby files this Complaint

against PJM. Mon Power respectfully requests, pursuant to Rules 206(b)(11) and (h) of the

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,4 , fast-track processing and expedited review by

the Commission.

 I.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       At a time when West Virginia customers already face high electricity prices for reasons

outside Mon Power’s control, those customers were harmed by approximately $145 million in

connection with Winter Storm Fern.5 Mon Power brings this case because the public record and

information available to Mon Power raise serious concerns about how PJM’s operational decisions

to advance schedule and commit gas-fired generation during Winter Storm Fern—in potential

violation or exceedance of PJM’s tariff—caused the largest net expense in Mon Power’s history.

After assessing a full record following discovery, the Commission should determine whether a

targeted remedy is warranted to alleviate any financial harm caused by PJM’s actions.

       As described below, PJM relied heavily on an advance-scheduling practice during Winter

Storm Fern, whereby it advance scheduled, committed, and/or issued manual operating and

dispatch instructions to a significant amount of gas-fired generation. In 2025, PJM told the

Commission that, in the original version of PJM’s advance-scheduling practice, PJM rarely pre-

scheduled resources before the Day-Ahead Market, did so primarily to address projected

transmission constraints, and did so manually. PJM further represented that, as its advance-

scheduling process evolved to mitigate operational risk (such as the potential that a gas-fired unit

could not obtain sufficient fuel) and not just transmission constraints, advance-scheduled resources

were made subject to Day-Ahead Market economic evaluation and received Day-Ahead Market

commitments only if they were part of the least-cost solution, i.e., they would be economically

evaluated. If they did not clear in the Day-Ahead Market, they could be ordered to run and receive

an uplift payment to make them whole. Mon Power has deep-seated concerns that this did not




5
  September 29, 2026 Affidavit of David Hunger (“Hunger Aff.”) (Exhibit No. MPC-0018) ¶¶ 8–
10, 27–29.
                                                 3
 happen here, or, at a minimum, did not happen consistent with PJM’s representations or happened

in a way that exacerbated poor market conditions.

        The participation of advance-scheduled resources in the Day-Ahead Market can potentially

increase clearing prices and uplift payments, and thus cause material costs to customers. During

Winter Storm Fern, more expensive gas generation appears to have been advance scheduled and

cleared in the Day-Ahead Market (or, if not cleared, was instructed by PJM to run and receive an

uplift payment), while Mon Power’s cheaper coal-fired generation often remained at or near

economic minimum. System energy prices were higher and congestion increased as well, which

in turn raised the total LMP in areas such as Mon Power’s load node and lowered the LMPs at the

nodes at which Mon Power’s coal-fired generators sold power.

        For example, during the early afternoon hours on January 28, 2026, Mon Power’s Harrison

units offered energy at approximately $50/MWh, yet PJM did not clear the units above their

economic minimum levels, even though the system energy component of LMP was approximately

$250/MWh.6      This phenomenon—Mon Power generation plants having lower-cost energy

available yet not being dispatched beyond their economic minimum levels—appears to have

occurred repeatedly during Winter Storm Fern. That outcome raises serious questions about PJM’s

advance-scheduling practice—questions only fulsome discovery can answer.

        The high system energy prices during Winter Storm Fern appear to reflect PJM’s heavy

reliance on otherwise economically uncompetitive natural gas generation. PJM has asserted that

advance scheduling was needed to give those gas-fired units the financial certainty required to

procure fuel more than a day before the operating day and to avoid potential fuel procurement

problems, but many of those resources already had an obligation to be available because they had

 cleared in the capacity market.7 Put another way, many of these units were already being paid to

be available and faced penalties if they were unavailable.8 Absent a showing that these units would

likely have failed to perform through normal market processes according to existing market rules,

PJM’s unprecedented gas-focused advance-scheduling actions were unnecessary and harmful.

PJM also appears to have materially erred in projecting load by failing to account for school,

business, and government closures during the severe winter storm.9 PJM may additionally have

failed to adequately reassess, reduce, or unwind its advance-scheduling decisions after those errors

and other real-world impacts became evident.

         PJM’s actions during Winter Storm Fern had severe congestion and price effects. Mon

Power’s coal generation was located upstream of relevant transmission constraints, while Mon

Power’s load was located downstream of those constraints. PJM’s apparently excessive advance

scheduling and commitment of gas generation may have materially changed generation patterns

and worsened congestion across those transmission constraints, depressing and driving negative

the LMPs paid to Mon Power’s coal-generation nodes while increasing the LMP Mon Power paid

to serve load.10 In this way, Mon Power’s retail customers were penalized for PJM’s actions

purporting to promote system-wide reliability.

        PJM’s response to Winter Storm Fern should not be immune from scrutiny merely because

PJM invokes “reliability” to justify it. While PJM may be entitled to exercise discretion leading

up to and during an emergency, that discretion must remain within the filed tariff and must be

exercised in a just, reasonable, non-discriminatory manner that is consistent with cost-causation

principles. The existing record provides strong reason to question whether PJM exceeded or

misapplied its narrow tariff authority, discriminated against non-gas resources such as coal, and

produced unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential outcomes that are

inconsistent with cost-causation principles. Mon Power and PJM conferred before the filing of

this Complaint but were unable to resolve the dispute. The Commission should set this Complaint

for hearing so that Mon Power can obtain the needed discovery, subject to the protections of the

Commission’s Model Confidentiality Agreement, and PJM’s actions can be evaluated.

II.    PARTIES

       A.     Complainant

       Mon Power is a FirstEnergy Corporation subsidiary and PJM market participant that serves

retail customers in West Virginia. Mon Power serves retail customer load by purchasing power

from the PJM market, and also sells power into the PJM market from its generation resources,

including the Fort Martin and Harrison coal-fired plants. As such, Mon Power occupies a dual

position in PJM’s markets: regarding its load, Mon Power pays PJM; regarding its generating

resources, Mon Power receives PJM market revenues when its units generate and sell energy into

the PJM market. Under ordinary conditions, Mon Power’s generation revenues help offset the

costs of serving its load, and there is typically no material divergence between the LMPs at Mon

Power’s generators’ nodes and the LMP at Mon Power’s load node.




                                               6
        During Winter Storm Fern, that relationship broke down. Mon Power’s coal generation

was located upstream of relevant transmission constraints, while Mon Power’s load was located

downstream. PJM’s apparently excessive advance scheduling of gas-fired generating units may

have caused or materially contributed to significant congestion, which depressed or drove negative

LMPs at Mon Power’s generation nodes while increasing the LMPs Mon Power paid to serve

load.11 Mon Power estimates that the divergence between the LMPs paid to serve load and the

LMPs received by its generation resulted in losses of approximately $145 million, net of Financial

Transmission Rights (“FTR”) revenues that partially offset congestion costs.

       Absent the Commission’s intervention, those losses will be borne by Mon Power’s retail

customers in West Virginia even though PJM claims to have taken its actions in the name of

ensuring reliability for all of PJM.

       B.      Respondent

       PJM is a Commission-jurisdictional regional transmission organization. PJM administers

the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff, Operating Agreement, Day-Ahead Market, Real-Time

Market, emergency operations, congestion management, uplift, Operating Reserve credits, and

related settlement processes. PJM’s practices affecting wholesale rates, uplift charges, dispatch,

market settlements, congestion, and reliability-related commitments are subject to the FPA,

including FPA sections 205, 206, and 309.

 III.      JURISDICTION AND LEGAL STANDARDS

          A.       FPA Section 206 Requires PJM To Comply With Its Filed Tariff

          This Complaint arises under the FPA, the Commission’s regulations, and the PJM Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM OATT”) and Operating Agreement (“PJM OA”) (the latter two

together, the “tariff”). Under Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, any

person may file a complaint seeking Commission action against another person alleged to have

violated a statute, rule, order, or other law administered by the Commission, or to have committed

any other wrong within the Commission’s jurisdiction.12

          FPA section 206(a) authorizes the Commission to determine whether “any rate, charge,

classification, [] rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate, charge, or classification”

is unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential.13 That authority includes the power

to determine whether a public utility, regional transmission organization, or other Commission-

jurisdictional entity violated or misapplied its existing filed tariff, and to order appropriate relief.

          To be clear, Mon Power is not alleging in this Complaint that the Commission should adopt

prospective tariff reforms. Rather, Mon Power alleges that PJM violated or acted beyond the

existing tariff.

          B.     PJM Is Required To Operate The Day-Ahead Market To Reach the Least-Cost
                Solution

         The PJM tariff establishes a centralized Day-Ahead Market and resource-commitment

process.14 That market is designed to commit and dispatch resources economically so that

customers receive the benefit of least-cost market clearing. PJM’s implementing market rules

confirm this requirement. For example, PJM Manual 11 explains that the Day-Ahead Market must

operate to “minimize[] the total production cost (subject to certain limitations) for energy and

reserves.”15 In other words, the Day-Ahead Market is intended to produce the least-cost solution.

         The Commission has likewise recognized that a central function of the PJM markets,

including the Day-Ahead Market, is to ensure just and reasonable rates by producing the least-cost

solution.16 That least-cost principle is directly implicated here because PJM represented to the

Commission in 2025 that advance-scheduled resources would remain subject to Day-Ahead

economic evaluation and would clear only if they were part of the least-cost solution.17 Although

PJM also represented that, to the extent needed for reliability, PJM could manually dispatch

advance-scheduled units that did not clear in the market and pay them uplift, that practice (as well

as the advance scheduling that precedes it) can result in higher-cost units running instead of lower-

cost units and therefore must be carefully evaluated.

         C.     The Tariff Grants PJM Limited Advance-Scheduling Authority

        PJM’s tariff foothold for advance scheduling is Operating Agreement Schedule 1

§ 1.10.1(d). That provision states that, if PJM’s “forecast for the next seven days projects a

likelihood of Emergency conditions,” PJM “may commit, for all or part of such seven day period,

to the use of generation resources with notification or start-up times greater than one day as

necessary in order to alleviate or mitigate such Emergency, in accordance with the Market Sellers’

offers for such units for such periods and the specifications in the PJM Manuals.” 18 This single

sentence is the only tariff provision that expressly gives PJM authority to advance schedule

generation resources.

        That authority is narrow. It applies only where PJM’s seven-day forecast projects likely

Emergency conditions; only to resources with notification or start-up times greater than one day;

and only to the extent the commitment is “necessary” to alleviate or mitigate the projected

Emergency. The provision does not give PJM broad, open-ended authority to schedule and to

commit resources in advance without regard to necessity, non-discrimination, congestion, cost-

causation, or other settlement consequences.

        Nor does the provision establish a comprehensive advance-scheduling regime. It does not

specify how PJM must select resources, how it must account for fuel type or location, how it must

consider cheaper available resources, how it must update schedules and commitments when

forecast conditions change, how advance scheduling and commitments must interact with Day-

Ahead Market clearing, or how resulting uplift and congestion costs must be allocated. Nor does

the tariff establish transparent criteria governing PJM’s pre-Day-Ahead Market operating

instructions or the circumstances under which resources scheduled in advance but not clearing the

 Day-Ahead Market may nevertheless receive operator-initiated or out-of-market commitments.

Those omissions underscore the limited nature of PJM’s authority and the need to determine

whether PJM’s Winter Storm Fern practices stayed within the tariff’s bounds.

         D.      PJM Must Exercise Its Advance-Scheduling Authority Consistently With
                 Least-Cost Market Principles

         PJM’s limited advance-scheduling authority must be exercised against the backdrop of the

tariff’s offer-based market structure and the Day-Ahead Market’s economic clearing function. As

noted above, PJM confirmed this point in a November 14, 2025 filing, stating that, prior to Winter

Storm Elliott, it rarely engaged in advance scheduling despite the authority to do so having been

in the PJM tariff since 1996.19 Indeed, PJM represented that “[p]rior to 2024, PJM rarely pre-

scheduled resources before the close of the Day-ahead Energy Market and did so primarily to

address projected transmission constraints.”20 PJM stated that its pre-Winter Storm Elliott practice

was to schedule in advance the minimum resources needed to address forecasted transmission

constraints, and that resources advance scheduled for that purpose were automatically included in

the Day-Ahead Market.21

           E.     PJM Is Required To Follow Practices That Are Non-Discriminatory And
                  Consistent With Cost-Causation Principles

           PJM’s tariff requires PJM to administer emergency practices on a non-discriminatory basis.

PJM OATT Attachment K-Appendix § 1.7.11 provides that PJM’s standards, policies, and

procedures for declaring, managing, alleviating, or ending an Emergency “shall apply to all

Members on a non-discriminatory basis.”27 Similarly, PJM OA Schedule 1 § 1.7.11 contains

parallel requirements. The FPA also requires jurisdictional rates and practices affecting rates to be

just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.28 Those requirements include

the Commission’s cost-causation principles, which require costs to be allocated in a manner

roughly commensurate with benefits received or burdens imposed.29

           PJM’s reliability-related uplift framework reflects the same principles.     PJM OATT

Attachment K-Appendix § 3.2.3(b)(i)(B) provides that, where PJM determines during reliability

analysis for an Operating Day that a resource was committed to maintain system reliability, the

associated balancing Operating Reserve credits, identified as “RA Credits for Reliability,” are

allocated according to each participant’s ratio share of real-time load (and to any transactions

selling to customers outside PJM). That rule recognizes that reliability commitments are system

        F. PJM Is Required To Exercise Good Utility Practice

        PJM’s emergency actions must also be consistent with Good Utility Practice.30 That

requirement independently constrains how PJM may exercise operational discretion during

emergency conditions.

        Good Utility Practice is defined in OA section 1 to include practices, methods, and acts

that, in the exercise of reasonable judgment in light of facts known at the time, could have been

expected to accomplish the desired result at reasonable cost consistent with good business

practices, reliability, safety, and expedition.31 Thus, even where PJM acts to preserve reliability, it

must exercise reasonable judgment based on known facts and at reasonable cost.

            Good Utility Practice also incorporates cost-causation principles. Specifically, because

Good Utility Practice requires accepted industry practices and reasonable cost, it must be read

consistently with the FPA’s cost-causation principles, which require that “all approved rates reflect

to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them.”32 The Commission

and federal courts therefore “scrutinize a utility’s rates to ensure a match between cost-causation

and cost-responsibility.”33 A practice is unjust and unreasonable and violates cost-causation

principles where there is “a sizable gap between the benefits accrued by each LSE [Load-Serving

Entity] and the allocated cost.”34

           Those principles apply here because PJM’s Winter Storm Fern actions appear to have

imposed extraordinary costs on Mon Power and its customers. For example, if PJM engaged in

excessive advance scheduling based on an overstated forecast, failed to adequately reassess,

reduce, or unwind those advance schedules and commitments as actual conditions changed,

displaced lower-cost available resources, worsened congestion, and then left the burden of the

resulting LMP-separation harm on Mon Power and its West Virginia customers, then PJM did not

exercise Good Utility Practice.

         H.      The Commission’s Remedial Authority

         If the Commission finds that PJM violated or misapplied the filed tariff, exceeded its tariff

authority, or administered tariff-governed practices in an unjust, unreasonable, unduly

discriminatory, preferential, or non-cost-causative manner, the Commission may order

and unfairness could have opened the door for possible market manipulation by natural gas

generators who were given advance knowledge they would be made whole regardless of how they

bid into the market. Indeed, PJM flagged the possibility of such conduct in its November 2025

filing, and whether it occurred here is another issue to explore during discovery.

       With the benefit of discovery, Mon Power expects to show that PJM’s advance scheduling,

commitment, and uplift treatment were unduly discriminatory and preferential under FPA section

206 and the PJM tariff.

       E.      PJM May Have Failed To Adequately Update Or To Unwind Its Forecast And
               Advance-Scheduling Strategy After Forecast Errors Became Evident

       PJM’s load forecast was materially overstated. PJM has acknowledged that its forecast did

not adequately account for closure effects, including school, business, and government closures


                                                49
 during the storm, and that actual system conditions diverged from forecasted conditions in part for

this reason.136

        That forecast error—which appears to be a methodological error—mattered because PJM’s

advance-scheduling authority, if any, was tied to necessity. PJM could justify advance scheduling

only to the extent it was necessary to alleviate or mitigate the forecasted emergency.

        Moreover, once actual conditions showed that PJM’s forecast was overstated, PJM was

obligated to reassess whether its advance scheduling remained necessary. At a minimum, PJM

should have reassessed its operational decisions once it became clear that, contrary to its forecast

assumptions, schools, businesses, and government offices were closing in response to the storm.

        Discovery is needed to assess whether PJM adequately did so. If it did not, then that failure

likely caused or materially contributed to excessive uplift, distorted dispatch, congestion, and LMP

separation affecting Mon Power.137

        PJM’s potential failure to adequately update its forecast and advance-scheduling strategy

as actual conditions diverged from forecasted conditions also supports the conclusion that PJM

misapplied its emergency authority and violated Good Utility Practice. Good Utility Practice

requires the exercise of reasonable judgment in light of facts known at the time.

        Discovery will allow Mon Power to obtain PJM’s forecast data, forecast updates, internal

communications, commitment studies, and operational analyses showing when PJM knew the

forecast was overstated and what, if anything, PJM did in response, including the timing, scope,

and basis for any unit-specific adjustments.




136
    PJM Cold Weather Operations (Exhibit No. MPC-0010) at 17 (attributing forecasting error to
“extended school/government closings”).
137
      Hunger Aff. (Exhibit No. MPC-0018) ¶¶ 36, 40–42.

                                                 50
            F.     PJM’s Advance Scheduling Appears To Have Caused Congestion And Price
                  Effects That Harmed Mon Power

           PJM’s advance-scheduling and commitment decisions appear to have changed generation

patterns and materially contributed to congestion during Winter Storm Fern, separating the LMPs

applicable to Mon Power’s load and generation.138 Specifically, Mon Power paid high, congestion-

influenced LMPs to serve its customers, while its Fort Martin and Harrison coal units received

depressed or negative generation-node LMPs.

           That LMP separation caused substantial harm. Mon Power estimates that the divergence

between the prices it paid to serve load and the prices its generation received caused approximately

$145 million in losses, net of FTR revenues. This harm was not caused by Mon Power’s conduct.

Mon Power’s units were available and able to generate, but PJM’s advance-scheduling and

commitment strategy appears to have caused the congestion that prevented Mon Power from

receiving the generation revenues that ordinarily would have offset most of the cost of serving its

load.139

           Further, PJM’s settlement treatment of that harm appears unjust and unreasonable. PJM

treated the gas-resource costs (of units that did not clear in the market but were ordered to run) as

uplift eligible for broad allocation, but left the related congestion harm on Mon Power. In other

words, PJM broadly socialized the costs needed to make whole advance-scheduled or advance-

committed gas resources, while leaving Mon Power and its customers to bear the localized price

effects caused by the same reliability strategy.

           PJM’s advance-scheduling and commitment decisions were undertaken for asserted

system-wide reliability purposes. If that scheduling was necessary to preserve system reliability,


138
      Austria Aff. (Exhibit No. MPC-0019) ¶¶ 11–13, 16–20, 23–27, 30–31.
139
      Id. ¶¶ 21–22; Hunger Aff. (Exhibit No. MPC-0018) ¶¶ 8–10, 24, 27–29, 36–39, 49–50.

                                                   51
 then the costs caused by advance scheduling should have been allocated consistently with system-

wide reliability cost-allocation and cost-causation principles.

         The tariff reflects that principle. PJM OATT Attachment K-Appendix § 3.2.3(b)(i)(B)

provides that reliability-related balancing Operating Reserve credits are allocated according to

each participant’s share of real-time load plus export transactions.140 That provision recognizes

that reliability commitments are system or regional actions and that the associated costs should be

allocated broadly, rather than imposed arbitrarily on a small subset of market participants.

         PJM did not apply that principle to the full cost of its Winter Storm Fern reliability strategy.

That settlement treatment caused Mon Power and its customers to pay twice. First, Mon Power

paid high load-side LMPs while facing depressed or negative generation-node LMPs (and

consequently reduced revenues) from Fort Martin and Harrison. Second, Mon Power paid uplift

charges used to make whole the advance-scheduled or advance-committed resources whose

operation contributed to the congestion and price separation that harmed Mon Power in the first

place.

         PJM’s practices and settlements during Winter Storm Fern therefore appear inconsistent

with Good Utility Practice and cost-causation principles. PJM is not exercising Good Utility

Practice when it administers the Tariff in a manner that creates unjust and unreasonable practical

effects, including “a sizable gap between the benefits accrued by each LSE and the allocated

cost.”141 That appears to be what happened during Winter Storm Fern.

         As shown above, PJM appears to have violated or misapplied the tariff, and acted without

tariff authority for the advance-scheduling and commitment practice it used.



140

141
      Verso Corp., 898 F.3d at 8.

        G.      Retrospective Relief Enforces The Filed Tariff And Does Not Violate The Filed-
               Rate Doctrine

       Mon Power does not seek revision of the PJM tariff in this proceeding.142 It seeks

enforcement of the filed tariff and correction of settlement consequences caused by PJM’s apparent

violation or misapplication of that tariff. The filed-rate doctrine does not bar the Commission from

enforcing the tariff as filed, correcting settlements affected by tariff violations, or ordering relief

necessary to remedy unjust, unreasonable, discriminatory, or non-cost-causative charges.

       If the Commission finds that PJM exceeded or violated its tariff authority, misapplied its

advance-scheduling rules, discriminated against non-gas resources, failed to administer the Day-

Ahead Market consistent with least-cost principles, and/or imposed non-cost-causative settlement

consequences on Mon Power, the Commission may order refunds, resettlement, reallocation, or

other remedial relief to enforce the filed tariff. Such relief would not change the historical tariff.

It would correct the consequences of PJM’s failure to administer the tariff lawfully.

       Although Mon Power acknowledges that, under Commission precedent, rerunning the

market is disfavored as part of a remedy, there are a variety of mechanisms that do not involve a

market re-run by which the Commission can provide financial relief to the West Virginia customers

harmed by PJM’s actions.




142
    This proceeding is focused on whether PJM violated the existing tariff and how to remedy the
harm suffered by Mon Power and its West Virginia retail customers. The question of whether
reforms to the tariff may be needed is best addressed in a separate proceeding.

       A.      Rules 206(b)(1) and (2): Identify and Explain How The Action or Inaction
               Violates Applicable Statutory Standards or Regulatory Requirements

       PJM’s Winter Storm Fern advance-scheduling and commitment practices, Day-Ahead

Market clearing treatment, forecast failures, uplift treatment, congestion effects, and settlement

treatment appear to have violated the PJM OATT and PJM OA and appear to have been unjust,

unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, and preferential under FPA section 206. PJM appears to have

exceeded or misapplied PJM OA Schedule 1 section 1.10.1(d) by using advance scheduling and

commitments on a scale and in a manner not authorized by the filed tariff. PJM further appears to

have violated its non-discrimination obligations under PJM OA Schedule 1 section 1.7.11 and PJM

OATT Attachment K-Appendix section 1.7.11 by favoring gas resources over non-gas resources

and shifting the resulting costs to Mon Power. PJM further acted unjustly and unreasonably by

imposing non-cost-causative settlement consequences by allocating formal uplift broadly while

leaving the related congestion harm embedded in localized LMP separation affecting Mon Power.

       B.      Rule 206(b)(3): Set Forth the Business, Commercial, Economic or Other Issues

West Virginia retail customers.

       The market design issue is significant.      PJM’s advance-scheduling and commitment

practice gives PJM substantial power to determine which resources receive commitment certainty

and cost recovery, which resources are displaced, and which loads bear the resulting costs.

• Some of these commitments were uneconomic and

• The PJM energy market is a daily market which procures
  energy and reserves on a day-ahead basis and in real

  Real-Time Energy/Reserve Markets.

          to be available to provide energy and reserves whenever

  made, or will make, the necessary investment to
  ensure the resource has the capability to provide
  energy when called upon by PJM.” (PJM CP Filing 205
  P22).

©2025    www.monitoringanalytics.com   24

  that it:

          investment to ensure the Capacity Resource has the
          capability for the entire relevant Delivery Year to provide
          energy at any time when called upon by the Office of the
          Interconnection;
        • Shall be capable of complying with the performance
          obligations specified in this Attachment DD of the Tariff
          and Schedule 1 of the Operating Agreement by the
          relevant Delivery Year [Operating Parameter Limits];”
        • (PJM CP Filing 205 P23)
©2025          www.monitoringanalytics.com   25

  removed.
• FERC argued that it was “concerned that significant
  aspects of the required representation are
  inappropriately vague and this ambiguity could incent
  well-performing resources to elect not to participate in
  the capacity market to avoid the risk of sanction”.
  (151 FERC ¶ 61,208 P95)
• In terms of requirements, without this provisions, CP
  reverted to the legacy capacity definition. Without this
  provision, any resource can and did become CP.
©2025     www.monitoringanalytics.com   26
         Operating Parameters – PJM Filing
• CP proposed operating parameter limits based on
  physical operating design.
• The main goal was to limit the uplift payments
  experienced in late Jan 2014 due to gas market
  inflexibility (CP PJM Filing 206 P7).
• Operating parameters would be unit specific based on
  the resources’ physical capabilities.
• Also, during Hot or Cold Weather Alerts, the sum of
  the notification and start times could not exceed 14
  hours and the notification time could not exceed 1
  hour.
©2025    www.monitoringanalytics.com   27
         Operating Parameters – PJM Filing
• These provisions were rejected by FERC and
  changed.
• FERC argued that “because PJM’s proposed revisions
  are based only on physical constraints and generic
  time restrictions that may prevent a resource from
  reflecting in its energy market offer certain parameter
  limitations caused by legitimate, non-physical
  constraints”. (151 FERC ¶ 61,208 P435)
• These provisions were modified to allow operating
  parameter limits based on contractual limits that
  cannot be rectified with other commercial alternatives.
©2025    www.monitoringanalytics.com   28
                                       End Result
• A Capacity Performance resource was supposed to be a
  superior product compared to the Capacity Resource that
  existed in 2014.
  • It was supposed to produce and maintain investments to
    perform better.
  • It was supposed to seek better fuel contractual arrangements.
• This has failed by having no clear requirements on what it
  means to be CP.
• Instead, any resource can be CP by facing the financial
  consequences of bad performance, but only during a PAI.

   ©2025    www.monitoringanalytics.com    29
                                          End Result
• Today, a Capacity Performance resource can be:
        • A resource that only has interruptible gas
        • A resource that only provides energy when the sun is out
        • A resource, not base load, that takes 48 hours to start
        • A resource with a 96 hour minimum run time
        • A resource that cannot start when temperatures are
          below 10ºF.
• When CP was envisioned, these would not qualify as
  providing “greater assurance of delivery of energy
  and reserves.”

©2025          www.monitoringanalytics.com    30
                                      End Result
• From a market perspective, PJM expects resource
  owners to bear all the performance risks and reflect their
  nonperformance financial risks in their capacity offers
  (i.e. CPQR).
• From an operational perspective, PJM is not willing to
  let resources face such risks. Instead PJM scheduled
  units at risk in advance instead of waiting for the DA
  market.
• PJM market design treats any resource as a capacity
  resource as long as it bears the risks from
  nonperformance but PJM actual operations prevents
  resources from bearing such risks.
 ©2025     www.monitoringanalytics.com    31
                                        Next Steps
• Accept the reality that PJM will have to make advance,
  out of market, decisions during critical days to reduce
  generation performance risks.

        or

• Require capacity resources to be able to start within
  the DA market timeframe or to be online when alerts
  are in place.


©2025        www.monitoringanalytics.com    32
                                        Next Steps
• Accept reality: Units that cannot start/operate within
  the Day-Ahead Energy Market timeframe (about 16
  hour time to start, 13:30 of the day before to 05:00 of
  the next day) have to be committed before the DA
  Market.

        or

• Define   capacity    resources:   Require  capacity
  resources to be able to start within 16 hours or be
  online when alerts are in place.
©2025        www.monitoringanalytics.com    33
                                    Accept Reality
• PJM will need a defined and transparent process for the
  commitment of units before the DA Market.
• The process must include:
  • Criteria defining when this is invoked
  • Energy offers development rules
  • Tools used to optimally schedule resources
  • Communications process for these commitments
  • Operating parameters review (temperature limits)
  • DA Market participation
  • Uplift changes to account for multiday net profits/losses.
  • Treatment of limited resources, dual fuel, demand response.
   ©2025      www.monitoringanalytics.com   34
               Define Capacity Resources
• Create minimum operational requirements for
  capacity resources to ensure that these resources can
  be committed by the DA Market.
• Units that cannot start based on the DA Market
  timeframe will be required to be online based on alerts
  invoked by PJM.




©2025    www.monitoringanalytics.com   35
                        Resource Adequacy
• Either way, PJM must reflect expected performance
  based on actions taken through conservative
  operations. Historical construct of ELCC fails to
  account for change in behavior from generators and
  from PJM operations.
• Either way, resources must have explicit operational
  requirements.
• These are significant changes but necessary to avoid
  overestimating risk now which will result in
  overprocurement in the future.

MPC-0003
                                                             Problem / Opportunity Statement

RESOURCE SCHEDULING PRIOR TO THE DAY AHEAD
ENERGY MARKET
PJM System Operators, at times, will schedule resources in advance of the Day-ahead Energy
Market based on projected system conditions that may warrant conservative resource scheduling.

The IMM has raised concerns about the lack of transparency regarding the process of scheduling
resources prior to the Day-Ahead Energy Market. These concerns include communication
process, offers used for commitment evaluation, use of operating parameters, and financial
consequences of commitment.

Also, resources scheduled in advance of the Day-ahead Energy Market have the opportunity to
submit updated bids prior to the next available Day-ahead Energy Market closing. Such resources
are offer capped in certain circumstances prior to the initiation of the Day-ahead case to mitigate
against the potential exercise of market power.

There is an opportunity to explore enhancements to the rules related to the commitment of
resources prior to the Day-ahead Energy Market.
